segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now concerning the collection for the holy ones: just as I directed the assemblies of Galatia, so you also are to do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the first day of every week, each of you is to set something aside and save it up at home, in proportion to how you have prospered, so that no collections have to be made when I come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when I arrive, I will send those you approve, with letters, to carry your gift to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if it is worthwhile for me to go as well, they will go with me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I will come to you after I pass through Macedonia—for I am going through Macedonia—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and perhaps I will stay with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on my way wherever I go.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for a great and effective door has opened for me, and there are many who oppose me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If Timothy comes, see that he can be with you without fear, for he is doing the Lord’s work, just as I am.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So let no one treat him with contempt. Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now concerning our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers, but he was not at all willing to come now; he will come when he has the opportunity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Stay alert, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let everything you do be done in love.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I urge you, brothers and sisters—you know the household of Stephanas, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the holy ones—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that you too submit to such people, and to everyone who shares in the work and labors at it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I rejoice at the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they have refreshed my spirit and yours. So give such people recognition.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The assemblies of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the assembly that meets in their house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All the brothers and sisters greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone does not love the Lord, let that person be accursed. Our Lord, come!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus.

notes.note: This is the fund Paul was gathering from his largely non-Jewish assemblies for the impoverished believers in Jerusalem. He also discusses it in Romans 15 and 2 Corinthians 8–9. The Greek word was an ordinary term for a collection of money, often for a religious purpose.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Here it refers specifically to the believers in Jerusalem. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The traditional rendering is “churches.” A first-century hearer knew this word as the ordinary term for a civic gathering and as the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. “Church” remains near-universal in English translations, and some find that “assembly” sounds like a one-off meeting.

notes.phrase: On the first day of every week
notes.traditional: Upon the first day of the week
notes.note: The Greek follows the Jewish way of counting days from the Sabbath, so the day meant is Sunday. This is one of the earliest indications that the first day of the week had special significance for believers. The instruction itself, however, is about each person setting money aside privately, not about an offering taken at a meeting.

notes.traditional: whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters, them will I send
notes.note: The phrase can attach to either verb. On the reading adopted here, Paul will send the approved delegates with letters of introduction; on the other, the Corinthians approve their delegates by letter. Most modern translations take the first view, since Paul would be present in Corinth and written approval from the Corinthians would be unnecessary.

notes.phrase: he was not at all willing
notes.traditional: his will was not at all to come at this time
notes.note: The Greek says only “it was not at all the will that he come now,” without saying whose will. Most translations take it as Apollos’s own unwillingness, which fits the following clause about his finding an opportunity. Some interpreters take it as God’s will, since the word used without qualification can have that sense.

The verb is formed from the word for “man,” and older translations render it “quit you like men” or “act like men.” In period usage, and repeatedly in the Septuagint alongside “be strong,” it simply means to show courage, and it is addressed here to the whole community. Several modern translations render it the same way.

The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members, and Paul is addressing the whole community, women included. Where the word refers to specific traveling companions (verses 11 and 12), “brothers” is kept. Some translations retain “brothers” throughout and explain the inclusive sense in a footnote.

Many translations have “ministry” here. In the first century this was an everyday word for serving someone or carrying out a task on another’s behalf, and it did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession. Some translations also use “service” in this verse.

This is the same Greek word used elsewhere for the “coming” of the Lord. Here it has its everyday sense of someone arriving and being present. “Arrival” is used for ordinary people to keep the two uses distinct.
Letters were normally dictated to a secretary. At this point Paul takes the pen himself and writes the closing lines, a common practice that served as a personal mark of authenticity.

Paul writes an Aramaic phrase in Greek letters without translating it, evidently a cry already familiar from the worship of the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers. Divided as “marana tha” it is a prayer, “Our Lord, come!”; divided as “maran atha” it would be a statement, “Our Lord has come.” Most scholars favor the prayer, which matches “Come, Lord Jesus” in Revelation 22:20. Older translations leave the phrase untranslated as “Maranatha.”

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (whole community) / brothers (specific companions)
candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translations split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so a single policy for the inclusive plural is needed.

Very frequent in Paul and Acts and rendered variously as urge, appeal, exhort, encourage and comfort; the sense boundaries should be fixed.
Recurs in the household codes, Romans 13 and elsewhere with “submit,” “be subject” and “be subordinate” as competing renderings that readers will notice.
